name: Chloe Usman

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hi Chloe, thanks for doing this. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or any political party. What you tell me is confidential, so feel free to say what you'd say in public and also what you really think. Could you start by describing a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Right now I'm on an office refit in the city centre, the sixth floor of an old insurance building. We strip it back and put in new stud walls, ceilings, doors, the lot, and I'm the junior carpenter on our firm's crew of five. Most days I'm fixing metal studs and plasterboard, or hanging doors with Dev, our foreman, checking every hinge I put on. I'm still slow on doors, if I'm honest.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How did you end up in the trade, and what do you like about it?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I was working in a café till I was twenty-four and I hated it, so I joined a scheme for women getting into construction. I left school without finishing, so it was that or more lattes. What I love is walking through a floor at the end of a job and knowing I built that corridor. What wears me out is the dust, the lifts never working, and the odd bloke who still asks if I'm the cleaner.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably post something like, see, the robots aren't coming for the chippies after all. At work Dev would be smug, he's always said AI is for people in suits. I'd say good, now let's talk about the real problems, like pay and the lack of decent toilets on site.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it means I can just focus on getting better at the job. I'd like my proper trade certificate in the next year or so, and then maybe run my own small crew one day. Nothing gets in the way except my own speed with doors.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on, basically. Finish the certificate, keep saving the bit I save now, I've got about three months of rent put by. I'd keep using the AI chat thing now and then to check a cutting list or tidy up an email to a client, but that's it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty good, actually. Calm, a bit like the future is still mine to mess up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned pay and site toilets as the real problems. Why bring those up here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because all this AI talk lets the bosses change the subject. Every meeting at the union women's network, we talk about not being able to find a toilet that locks, and nobody fixes it. If AI turns out to be nothing, maybe we can get back to that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you use the AI tool much now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe once a week. My housemate Jess showed me, and I use it to double-check maths when Dev's not around, because I don't want to look stupid asking twice. It's handy, like a calculator that talks back. I'm not going to build my life around it.

S0.say: I'd post that the robots aren't coming for carpenters after all. Then I'd say let's get back to real problems like pay and decent site toilets.
S0.think: Privately it means she can focus on getting better at the job and getting her trade certificate. Maybe one day she runs her own small crew.
S0.do: Carries on at the office refit firm, finishes her trade certificate and keeps saving as she does now. Keeps using the AI chat tool about once a week to check cutting lists and emails.
S0.feel: Calm and pleased, as if the future is still hers to shape.
S0.quote: It's handy, like a calculator that talks back. I'm not going to build my life around it.
S0.fieldNote: Chloe sees AI talk partly as a distraction from everyday fairness issues for women on site. She uses AI quietly to avoid asking twice, which says something about how exposed she feels as a junior woman on a crew. Her ambition is concrete: certificate, then her own small crew.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say workers need a seat at the table when firms decide what gets automated, and the government should pay for retraining, not leave it to bosses. Online I'd share the union line. I'd also say make sure women don't get pushed out first, because we always are.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think fit-out is one of the places that changes. There's already a robot that draws the wall lines on the floor from the plans, Dev saw one on a big job. If the setting-out goes to a machine, the junior who does the fiddly bits is a bit exposed, and that's me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the firm to send me on whatever course comes with the new kit, and I'd push through the union for it to be paid time. I'd use the AI stuff more, properly this time, maybe get Jess to show me how to read plans with it. And I'd try to get from three months saved up to five.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. I'm not panicking, but I'd be watching who gets let go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said women always get pushed out first. Is that from experience?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: On my last job, when the work slowed, the agency girl and I were the first two moved to snagging, which is just fixing other people's mistakes. Two blokes with less time on site kept the good work. Nobody said why, they never do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dev, weirdly. He's brilliant but he won't touch a tablet, and he's fifty-one. If the firm wants someone who can run the new gear, it might be me over him, and I'd hate that. I'd rather we learned it together.

S1.say: I'd say workers need a say in what gets automated and government should pay for retraining. Online I'd share the union line and warn that women mustn't be pushed out first.
S1.think: Privately she thinks fit-out changes a lot, with setting-out going to machines. As the junior doing fiddly bits, she feels exposed.
S1.do: Asks the firm for paid training on any new kit and pushes for it through the union. Uses AI tools more seriously and raises her savings from about three months to five.
S1.feel: Uneasy, watching who gets let go.
S1.quote: If the firm wants someone who can run the new gear, it might be me over him, and I'd hate that.
S1.fieldNote: Her worry about being pushed out is rooted in a specific experience of being moved to snagging first. Interestingly she imagines she might outlast her foreman because he won't touch tech, and that troubles her. She is ready to learn once the change is visible on site.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be loud about it. I'd say this is the moment governments have to step in, pay people while there's no work, tax the companies that own the robots. Online I'd be sharing every campaign, and at work I'd be telling everyone to join the union now, before it's too late.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I think I'm done in that picture. I'd only just have my certificate, and a robot that can hang a door better than me in two years? It took me three years to even get on site. That's what hurts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can. Keep in mind there are only about 2 years before it arrives.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First I'd stop spending on anything I don't need, no takeaways, no festival this summer, and get my savings as high as I can, maybe four months. I'd go hard on the union side, organising, marches, the lot. Once it arrives, I'd move back in with my mum if I had to, she's got a spare room above her shop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. Like I've climbed a ladder and someone's taking the rungs out above me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With two years, would you try to learn anything new?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know what I'd learn. In the slow picture you learn to work alongside the robot, but here the robot doesn't need you. I'd probably finish my certificate anyway, out of stubbornness, and because I'd want something to show for the last three years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your mum when you moved back?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm sorry, Mum, I did everything right this time. She's always said I'd find my thing, and I did. I think she'd make me work in the shop, and I'd let her.

S2.say: I'd say governments must step in now, pay people with no work and tax the companies that own the robots. I'd tell everyone at work to join the union before it's too late.
S2.think: Privately she thinks she's done: a robot that hangs doors better than her in two years undoes three years of fighting to get on site. That's what hurts most.
S2.do: Cuts all non-essential spending to build savings to around four months and throws herself into union organising and protests. Plans to move back in with her mum above the shop if work disappears.
S2.feel: Alarmed, like climbing a ladder while someone removes the rungs above her.
S2.quote: I'd say I'm sorry, Mum, I did everything right this time.
S2.fieldNote: The two-year picture hits her sense of having finally earned a place after a hard road in. Her politics sharpen and turn outward, while her private plan is retreat to family. Finishing the certificate 'out of stubbornness' shows how much the trade means to her identity.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough time to plan, so there's no excuse for anyone being thrown on the scrapheap. I'd push for the union to get a deal with the big contractors on retraining and notice periods.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, five years gives me a chance I didn't have in the fast one. I'd still lose carpentry as I know it, but I could get into whatever comes next before the rush. I'd be thirty-two, still young enough to start again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can. This time there are about 5 years of warning.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish my certificate this year, then look for a course in running and maintaining the building robots, once I see a few people I know doing it. I'd use the AI tools daily, not weekly, to practise. And I'd keep saving, maybe aim for six months by year three.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but more in control. It's a race I might win.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd wait to see people you know doing it. Why not go first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I've been burned. I did a fancy online course once, before the women's scheme, and it was useless, I paid for it myself. I'd want to see someone like me get a real job out of it before I spend my savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the one thing you'd want sorted in those five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Proper money for retraining that doesn't come out of my savings. If they gave me a wage to study for a year, I'd go in a heartbeat. Without that I'd be doing it at night after a day carrying plasterboard, and I know how that ends.

S3.say: I'd say five years is enough time to plan, so nobody should be thrown on the scrapheap. I'd push the union to win retraining and notice deals with big contractors.
S3.think: Privately she sees a chance to get into the next kind of work before the rush. At thirty-two she'd still be young enough to start again.
S3.do: Finishes her trade certificate this year, then takes a course in running and maintaining building robots once she sees others succeed. Uses AI tools daily and aims for six months of savings by year three.
S3.feel: Anxious but more in control, like a race she might win.
S3.quote: I'd want to see someone like me get a real job out of it before I spend my savings.
S3.fieldNote: Five years turns her from defensive to strategic. Her caution about going first comes from paying for a useless online course before, not from fear of tech. She wants paid study time and sees night classes after site work as a trap.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the last one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the best chance we'll ever get to do it fairly. Ten years means proper planning, so I'd be pushing for shorter weeks and retraining with a wage, and I'd say it online and at union meetings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, ten years feels manageable. I'd get maybe eight good years as a carpenter, run a small crew, and still have time to move into something else before it lands. I'd be thirty-seven, which isn't old.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can. This time there are about 10 years of warning.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd do what I'm doing now and finish the certificate. Around year three or four, once the robots start showing up on real sites, I'd move into something like site technician, the person who sets the machines up and checks their work. I'd get active in the union too, maybe as a rep, because ten years is long enough to change the rules.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but I can live with it. It's far enough away to make a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything ten years would let you do that five wouldn't?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Have my own crew first. That was always the dream, my own little all-women fit-out team. With ten years I might get to do it for a few years before it changes, and that would matter to me even if it doesn't last.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Some people say the long warning makes it easy to put things off. Would you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably a bit, yeah. I'd tell myself I'll start the course next year for about three years. But I'd hope seeing it on site would wake me up.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is the best chance to make the change fair. I'd push for shorter weeks and paid retraining, online and at union meetings.
S4.think: Privately ten years feels manageable: eight good years as a carpenter, maybe running a small crew, and time to switch before it arrives. She'd be thirty-seven, not old.
S4.do: Finishes her certificate in the first year and keeps working as a carpenter. Moves into a site technician role setting up and checking machines around year three or four, and becomes active as a union rep.
S4.feel: Uneasy but able to live with it, since there's time to plan.
S4.quote: That was always the dream, my own little all-women fit-out team.
S4.fieldNote: The long horizon brings back her dream of an all-women fit-out crew, even if only for a few years. She is honest that she'd procrastinate. Her shift into a technician role is planned around seeing robots on real sites, consistent with her wait-for-proof habit.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. I'd lose the trade I fought to get into before I even had my feet under me. What would help is a wage while I retrain, and a union with real teeth so people like me aren't the first out the door.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask who gets to learn the new stuff first. If it's always the lads who get sent on the course, women will be pushed out of construction again just as we got in. Somebody should be counting that.

headlineQuote: If it's always the lads who get sent on the course, women will be pushed out of construction again just as we got in.
portrait: Chloe Usman is a 27-year-old junior carpenter on office refits, who left a café job through a women-in-construction scheme and is working towards her trade certificate. She has about three months of rent saved, uses AI now and then to check her maths, and is active in her union's women's network. She is calm if AI fizzles and uneasy with steady change, watching who gets let go first. AGI in two years alarms her because it would undo the place she fought for; with five or ten years she becomes strategic, aiming for a site technician role once she sees others make it work.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, because she'd lose the trade she fought to get into before she was settled in it.
whatWouldHelp: A wage while she retrains, and a strong union so women and juniors aren't the first out the door.
